newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac seeks to revive election campaign.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac seeks to revive election campaign.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac prepared on Tuesday an effort to kick-start his centre-right government's lacklustre election campaign as the opposition left said it was in striking distance of an upset win.

Chirac's office confirmed he would publish an article in 14 regional dailies on Wednesday, from Lille in the north to Nice in the south, in a risky effort to nudge bored voters into backing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition.

The Socialists ridiculed Chirac's planned intervention, on the second anniversary of his election as president, and seized on polls showing the centre-right's lead in the race for the May 25-June 1 National Assembly election had all but evaporated.

"Things are open. The movement is even a little bit in our favour," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on a trip to Brittany, predicting the French voters might well confound Chirac's drive to get his allies re-elected.
Speculation about what Chirac would write put the campaign on hold as debate again veered towards personalities and away from issues such as record unemployment of 12.8 percent.
"Nobody doubts Chirac will vote RPR," said Daniel Vaillant, the Socialists' number two, referring to the Gaullist Rally for the Republic party Chirac founded and which is now led by Juppe.
"If Mr Juppe is calling for help from Mr Chirac, it means his campaign isn't going very well," he told Europe 1 radio.

Many politicians said Chirac needed to explain more clearly his decision to call the election almost 10 months early -- he has said France needs a new impulse partly to help it join a single currency from a position of strength.

But the election has allowed the left and far right to accuse Chirac of having a secret agenda of unpopular austerity measures to help qualify for the currency from 1999, or of wanting to pre-empt emerging sleaze scandals.

"The problem today is that France needs time to reform," Defence Minister Charles Millon said, explaining Chirac's April 21 dissolution of the National Assembly and welcoming his plan to intervene. "There's no question of changing course."
Chirac, elected to a seven-year term in 1995, is meant to be above day-to-day politics, but presidents often seek to use the prestige of their office to sway voters behind their allies.
However, Chirac could end up as a virtual lame duck for five years if voters ignore his advice and elect the opposition.
The Paris stock market and bonds dipped on Tuesday, unsettled by polls showing the race tightening. The CAC French share index ended 0.8 percent down.

The latest opinion polls of voting intentions on Monday showed the two sides almost level. A BVA survey gave the conservatives 40 percent, half a point ahead of the combined left, while a Louis Harris poll saw them level on 38 percent.
Both polls predicted the centre-right would retain a sharply reduced majority in parliament.
Britain's new Foreign Secretary Robin Cook was to make his first foreign trip on Wednesday to Paris, meeting Jospin as well as Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

Jospin hailed British Prime Minister Tony Blair's landslide victory last week. Taken together, the British Labour victory and a French Socialist win would "have major repercussions in Europe and happily shape its future", he said.
Writing in the Evenement du Jeudi weekly, he rejected claims by Chirac's allies that Blair's Labour party was a centrist party with far more modern and free-market views than his.

"Labour's programme is a programme of the moderate left, less bold than ours on some points, perhaps because Britain has fewer unemployed people than we have, even though it has more poor people," Jospin wrote.
Among the French Socialists' more radical plans are to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay.
